Gubernatorial From vision to abandonment: Nigeria’s unfinished development, By Dipo Baruwa Addressing this issue requires a deliberate and coordinated approach, one that is devoid of political bias. by Premium Times October 26, 2026 Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Add us on Google …addressing Nigeria’s challenge of abandoned projects demands more than increased funding or renewed political rhetoric. It requires systemic reform anchored in strong authority, effective coordination, well-aligned incentives, and unwavering commitment. By embedding these principles into the country’s development framework, Nigeria stands a better chance of breaking the cycle of unfinished ambitions, both physical and programmatic, and beginning the process of realising the full economic and social value of its investments.
The drive for socio-economic development has seen Nigeria embark on several developmental projects, ranging from physical infrastructure to economic programmes. These initiatives, on the face value, were often well articulated; designed to address strategic gaps in the country’s socio-economic landscape or to deepen the capacity for growth through new opportunities.
Unfortunately, a significant number of these projects have never seen the light of day. Some were abandoned before completion, while others have been left in a state of prolonged inactivity; effectively maintained in a form of ‘suspended animation’. As a result, unfinished structures dot the landscape across the country; some are completed facilities that never became commercially viable, while others remain trapped indefinitely between conception and construction. Several continue to receive annual budgetary allocations, even though they produce little or no public value.
The true cost of these projects, therefore, extends far beyond what was originally budgeted or already spent. It includes the recurring expenses of maintaining dormant institutions, the escalating cost of eventual completion, and the lost productive capacity, employment opportunities, and private investment that these projects were intended, but failed, to generate. Nigeria’s abandoned projects cannot, therefore, be understood through a single headline figure. They represent monumental undertakings that have continued to drain the economy both financially and psychologically, denying the country the benefits of a healthy, prosperous, and development-driven socio-economic environment.
Importantly, this challenge is not limited to physical infrastructure alone. A number of non-physical initiatives – economic programmes, policy interventions, and reform agendas – have also suffered similar fates. Many of these programmes were designed to stimulate growth, enhance productivity, or support vulnerable sectors, but were either prematurely discontinued, inconsistently implemented, or allowed to fade without achieving scale. The consequence is a significant loss of economic gains that could have been realised through scaling effects and multiplier impacts across sectors. In many cases, these abandoned or under-implemented programmes represent missed opportunities for sustained economic transformation, as their intended ripple effects across employment, income generation, and private sector development were never fully realised.
To fully grasp the scale and implications of this challenge, it is important to examine not only the financial outlays but also the systemic issues that have contributed to the persistence of these unfinished ambitions. Weak project planning, inconsistent policy direction, inadequate funding structures, corruption, and poor accountability mechanisms have all played significant roles. In many cases, changes in political leadership have led to shifts in priorities, resulting in the discontinuation or neglect of ongoing projects. A question that naturally arises is: why does the continued allocation of funds to such projects persist? While some may argue that allocation does not necessarily translate to disbursement, it nonetheless represents a diversion of scarce resources from other initiatives that could better align with the objectives of the incumbent administration and may have contributed to the high rate of budget non-completion recently experienced.
… strengthening institutional frameworks for project planning, execution, and monitoring is essential. Here lies the responsibility of the Federal Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning, with the National Infrastructure Integrated Master Plan serving as a central institutional instrument. Transparent procurement processes, clear accountability structures, and consistent policy implementation remain critical to ensuring that future projects and programmes are not subjected to the same fate.
Addressing this issue requires a deliberate and coordinated approach, one that is devoid of political bias. First, there is a need for a comprehensive audit of all abandoned projects undertaken by the government, federal or state, within the last two decades, to determine their current status, viability, and potential for completion or repurposing. This audit should also extend to major economic programmes and policy initiatives that have been discontinued or under-implemented, in order to capture the full spectrum of lost economic value. Projects and programmes that remain economically and socially relevant should be prioritised for completion or revival, while those that are no longer viable should be formally discontinued to prevent further waste of public resources.
Second, strengthening institutional frameworks for project planning, execution, and monitoring is essential. Here lies the responsibility of the Federal Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning, with the National Infrastructure Integrated Master Plan serving as a central institutional instrument. Transparent procurement processes, clear accountability structures, and consistent policy implementation remain critical to ensuring that future projects and programmes are not subjected to the same fate. By adopting a more disciplined and strategic approach to development planning, Nigeria can begin to reverse the trend of abandoned initiatives and unlock the economic potential that these investments were originally intended to deliver.

To better illustrate the scale, diversity, and implications of these unfinished ambitions, the table below presents a selection of notable projects across different sectors. It highlights their intended purpose, estimated costs, current status, and the economic opportunities that have been lost or deferred as a result of their prolonged inactivity.
Beyond the financial and sectoral overview provided above, it is also important to recognise that not all “abandoned” projects are the same. They differ in form, stage of development, and the nature of their failure. The classification below provides a framework for analysing these projects which could help in identifying appropriate policy responses.
At its core, the persistence of abandoned projects in Nigeria reflects deeper governance failures that can be understood through the lenses of authority, coordination, incentives, and commitment. The tragedy of Nigeria’s development is not that it lacks vision, but that it has not built the political and institutional capability to consistently translate vision into completion.
This classification underscores that each category of project failure requires a distinct policy response; while some projects may require renewed funding and completion, others may need restructuring, concessioning, or outright discontinuation. Without such differentiation, policy interventions risk being ineffective or misdirected.
From the tables above, it is apparent that the inglorious act of project abandonment has no boundary or sectoral limitation; it cuts across the fabric of the economy, with no sector or region spared. This reality extends beyond physical infrastructure to include economic programmes whose discontinuation has equally deprived the economy of growth momentum and multiplier benefits. While the figures cited are indicative and based on publicly accessible information at the time of writing, what remains undeniable is the continued accumulation of these colossal costs while the country grapples with severe socio-economic infrastructure deficits. It is also important to note that the projects highlighted exclude the thousands of educational, health, and social infrastructure facilities that have deteriorated due to poor maintenance and inadequate resource allocation, further compounding the scale of the challenge.
At its core, the persistence of abandoned projects in Nigeria reflects deeper governance failures that can be understood through the lenses of authority, coordination, incentives, and commitment. The tragedy of Nigeria’s development is not that it lacks vision, but that it has not built the political and institutional capability to consistently translate vision into completion. In this context, authority speaks to the clarity of institutional mandates and the ability of designated agencies to make and enforce decisions without undue political interference. Coordination highlights the need for alignment across ministries, departments, and agencies, as well as between federal and state governments, to ensure continuity and coherence in project execution. Incentives must be redesigned so that public officials are rewarded for completing projects efficiently and held accountable for delays, cost overruns, or abandonment. Finally, commitment requires a long-term policy orientation that transcends electoral cycles, ensuring that projects and programmes are seen through to completion regardless of changes in political leadership.
In conclusion, addressing Nigeria’s challenge of abandoned projects demands more than increased funding or renewed political rhetoric. It requires systemic reform anchored in strong authority, effective coordination, well-aligned incentives, and unwavering commitment. By embedding these principles into the country’s development framework, Nigeria stands a better chance of breaking the cycle of unfinished ambitions, both physical and programmatic, and beginning the process of realising the full economic and social value of its investments. Development is ultimately about state capability.
